summary: Defines a profile of TLS 1.2 that conforms to the NSA Suite B cryptography guidelines, with a transitional profile for TLS 1.0 and 1.1. This is a historic document, and it was replaced by RFC 6460.

eli5.summary: A government has a short list of approved secret-keeping recipes. This memo says how to use only those recipes in a secure web connection. A newer memo replaced it.

questions: what is suite b for tls
subtitle: NSA-approved cryptography for Transport Layer Security

tldr.problem: Organizations need TLS connections that use only cryptographic algorithms approved by government security guidelines.
tldr.mechanism: Suite B defines two security levels and specifies which cipher suites, elliptic curves, and signature algorithms must be used in TLS 1.2, with transitional rules for TLS 1.0 and 1.1.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is historic and replaced by RFC 6460.

sections.title: Suite B for Secure Connections
sections.content:
RFC 5430 defines how to use the United States National Security Agency's Suite B cryptography in TLS (Transport Layer Security), the protocol that secures web connections and other network communications. The RFC specifies a Suite B compliant profile for TLS 1.2 that uses only Suite B algorithms, and a transitional profile for TLS 1.0 and 1.1 that uses Suite B algorithms as much as possible for backward compatibility.

Suite B defines two security levels: 128-bit and 192-bit. At the 128-bit level, TLS uses 256-bit elliptic curves and 128-bit AES. At the 192-bit level, it uses 384-bit elliptic curves and 256-bit AES.
sections.eli5: This tells secure web connections how to pick math tricks and secret codes from an approved list, in two strength levels.

sections.title: Suite B Requirements
sections.content:
Suite B mandates that key establishment and authentication use Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC), while encryption uses Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). The RFC specifies that at the 128-bit security level, implementations use the secp256r1 (also called P-256) elliptic curve with AES-128, SHA-256, and ECDSA for signatures. At the 192-bit level, they use secp384r1 (P-384) with AES-256, SHA-384, and ECDSA.

For TLS 1.2, Suite B compliant implementations MUST support GCM (Galois Counter Mode) cipher suites when both client and server support them, falling back to CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) mode when necessary. For TLS 1.0 and 1.1, which do not support GCM, only CBC cipher suites are available.
sections.eli5: Pick the 256-bit or 384-bit curve math. Use AES and ECDSA. For new connections, use GCM if you can, otherwise CBC.

sections.title: Cipher Suites and Key Exchange
sections.content:
For the 128-bit security level at TLS 1.2, Suite B compliant clients MUST offer TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA256 in that order. For backward compatibility with TLS 1.0 and 1.1 servers, they MAY also offer TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA.

For the 192-bit level, the corresponding cipher suites use AES-256 and SHA-384. Servers MUST accept the highest priority Suite B cipher suite offered by the client and use the matching signature algorithms. The RFC permits Suite B compliant implementations to interoperate with non-Suite B servers by offering additional cipher suites.

All Suite B cipher suites use ECDHE (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral) key exchange with ECDSA signatures, meaning both are based on elliptic curve math.
sections.eli5: The client and server pick from a short list of approved combinations in order of strength. They use temporary elliptic-curve math to agree on a secret, then sign everything with ECDSA.

sections.title: Certificates and Signatures
sections.content:
Certificates used in Suite B connections MUST be signed with ECDSA. For the 128-bit level, the server's public key MUST use the P-256 curve, and the certificate signature MUST use either P-256 with SHA-256 or P-384 with SHA-384. For the 192-bit level, both the public key and signature MUST use P-384 with SHA-384.

When mutual authentication is used (client certificates), the same signature requirements apply to client certificates. The RFC also specifies which signature algorithms clients must offer in the signature_algorithms extension during the TLS handshake. At the 128-bit level, clients MUST offer SHA-256 with ECDSA. At the 192-bit level, they MUST offer SHA-384 with ECDSA.
sections.eli5: Certificates say who you are and are signed to prove it. Suite B certificates use ECDSA signing and the right elliptic curve for each security level.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Interoperability
sections.content:
Suite B TLS implementations may be configured to accept cipher suites outside Suite B for backward compatibility with older systems. However, when a Suite B compliant client and server connect to each other, they MUST use only Suite B cipher suites, ensuring consistent cryptographic strength.

A Suite B compliant client that also needs to interoperate with non-Suite B servers MAY offer additional cipher suites after the Suite B ones in the ClientHello message. Similarly, servers may accept non-Suite B cipher suites as a last resort when Suite B cipher suites are not offered.

The transitional profile for TLS 1.0 and 1.1 permits the use of CBC-only cipher suites since those TLS versions do not support GCM, providing a path toward eventual migration to TLS 1.2 with GCM.
sections.eli5: When two Suite B programs talk, they use Suite B recipes. But they can offer other recipes too, so they can talk to older programs.
